stimuli.title: Growing More Than Vegetables
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On a corner lot in many American cities, where a laundromat once stood or a house burned down years ago, you may now find rows of tomato cages, a hand-painted sign, and a shed full of borrowed tools. Community gardens, shared plots of land that neighbors farm together, have spread rapidly in recent decades. Supporters say they do far more than grow food. Skeptics point out that many gardens struggle to last.

[2] The idea is not new. During both world wars, the federal government urged Americans to plant “victory gardens” in backyards, schoolyards, and city parks so that more of the nation's commercial harvest could be sent to troops and allies. By some estimates, victory gardens supplied as much as 40 percent of the fresh vegetables Americans ate in 1944. After the war ended, most of these gardens disappeared. The modern movement began in the 1970s, when residents of struggling city neighborhoods started clearing trash from abandoned lots and planting them.

[3] The most obvious benefit is fresh food. In neighborhoods without a full-service grocery store, a garden plot can supply produce that would otherwise require a long bus ride to buy. A single well-tended 10-by-10-foot plot can yield dozens of pounds of vegetables in a season, and gardeners often share their extra harvest with neighbors, food pantries, and senior centers.

[4] Researchers have also looked for benefits that are harder to weigh. In one study, a team surveyed 400 adults in a mid-sized city, about half of whom belonged to a community garden. The gardeners reported eating more vegetables, exercising more, and knowing more of their neighbors by name than the non-gardeners did. The researchers noted, however, that people who choose to join a garden may already be more active and more social than people who do not, so the garden itself may not be responsible for all of the differences.

[5] Gardens can change a block in other ways, too. A vacant lot that once collected broken glass becomes a place where people gather after work. Children learn where food comes from. Older residents who grew up on farms find themselves teaching younger neighbors how to stake beans or save seeds. On some blocks, neighbors say a garden has replaced a spot where people once dumped old tires and mattresses.

[6] Yet many gardens do not survive. The biggest problem is land. Most community gardens are built on land the gardeners do not own, often vacant lots borrowed from a city or a private owner. When property values rise, owners may decide to sell or build, and a garden that took a decade to establish can be bulldozed in a day. Gardens also depend on volunteers. When the two or three people who organize work days and collect fees move away, a garden can fall apart within a season or two.

[7] Some cities have responded by protecting gardens in their zoning laws or by transferring lots to land trusts, nonprofit organizations that hold property permanently for community use. Others offer long-term leases in exchange for basic upkeep. These steps do not guarantee success, but they give gardeners a reason to invest in soil, sheds, and fruit trees that take years to pay off.

[8] A community garden will not end hunger or fix every problem in a neighborhood. But for the price of some seeds, a water line, and a secure claim to the land, it can turn an empty lot into one of the most productive places on the block.

stimuli.title: The Deep End
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The public pool opened at noon, but by eleven-thirty Marcus had already changed into his swim trunks twice. The first pair, he said, felt too loose. The second pair was the first pair again.

[2] “You're stalling,” I told him.

[3] “I'm getting ready.” He was nine and believed that if he said something calmly enough, it became true.

[4] The swim test was simple, at least on paper. To earn the green wristband that let a kid swim in the deep end, you had to tread water for one minute and then swim one length of the pool without touching the bottom or the wall. Every one of Marcus's friends had a green band. He had failed the test twice in June. I had promised our mother I would get him through it before school started, and school started on Tuesday.

[5] At the pool, the water lay flat and bright under the August sun, a sheet of hammered tin. The lifeguard, a tall girl with a whistle on a purple cord, wrote Marcus's name on her clipboard and pointed at the ladder. “Whenever you're ready.”

[6] Marcus climbed down three rungs and stopped with the water at his chest. He held the rail with both hands.

[7] “Let go,” I said. “You know how to do this. We practiced all week.”

[8] “In the shallow end.”

[9] “Water is water, Marcus.”

[10] He looked at me then, and I recognized the look, though it took me a second to remember where I had seen it. It was mine. Eight years earlier, I had stood on that same ladder, gripping that same rail, while my father crouched on the deck above me. I had been sure that the deep end was a different kind of water, heavier and darker, that it wanted to pull me down. My father had not told me water was water. He had climbed into the pool in his work clothes, boots and all, and floated beside me on his back with his arms spread wide, looking up at the sky as if he had all afternoon.

[11] “See?” he had said. “It holds you up. You just have to let it.”

[12] I had forgotten that. Or I had folded it away somewhere, the way you fold away a coat in summer and forget you own it.

[13] I kicked off my sandals. I was still wearing my shorts and T-shirt. The lifeguard raised an eyebrow, but she did not blow her whistle. I sat on the edge of the pool and slid in beside the ladder, and the cold closed over my shoulders like a hand. Then I leaned back, spread my arms, and let my feet rise until I was floating, my ears under the surface so that the noise of the pool turned soft and far away.

[14] After a while I felt the water shift. Marcus had let go of the rail with one hand. Then the other. He was paddling, stiff and choppy, his chin raised high, his eyes fixed on me.

[15] “Is it a minute yet?” he gasped.

[16] The lifeguard checked her watch. “Forty seconds.”

[17] He kept going. I stayed where I was, on my back, and said nothing at all, which was the hardest thing I did that summer.

[18] When the lifeguard called “Time,” Marcus turned and began to swim toward the far wall, slow and crooked, splashing more than he needed to. He did not look back at me once. I decided that was all right.

[19] That night he fell asleep with the green band still on his wrist. I sat at the kitchen table and called my father, who lived three states away now, and when he asked what was new, I told him about the pool. He was quiet for a moment. Then he laughed. “Boots and all,” he said. “I'd forgotten that.”

[20] “I hadn't,” I said, which was not exactly true, but it was true now.

stimuli.title: Lock the Clock on Daylight Saving Time
stimuli.source: By Carla Benson, shop owner and president of a downtown merchants association. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Twice a year, Americans go through a ritual that makes less sense every year. In March, we lose an hour of sleep. In November, we get it back, and evening darkness falls before many of us have left work. It is time to end the switch for good and make daylight saving time permanent.

The switch itself is dangerous. A large study of U.S. traffic deaths found that fatal crashes rose by about 6 percent in the week after clocks spring forward, when drivers are short on sleep. A study of hospitals in Michigan found more heart attacks on the Monday after the spring change. Every year we accept these risks for no good reason.

Permanent daylight saving time would also give us brighter evenings all year. Evening light is when people actually live their lives: kids play outside after school, families take walks, and people run errands after work. More light in the evening means more customers on Main Street. A survey by a national retail association found that 7 out of 10 shoppers say they are more likely to stop at a store on the way home when it is still light outside.

Brighter evenings may make streets safer, too. Some researchers have found that robberies drop when there is more daylight in the evening, since many crimes happen after dark.

I have seen the difference myself. Every November, the week after we “fall back,” foot traffic in my shop drops sharply. My regular customers tell me they just want to get home before dark. In June, those same customers linger for an hour.

Americans are ready for this change. In 2022, the U.S. Senate passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent without a single senator objecting. Nearly 20 states have passed similar laws and are waiting only for Congress to act. When this many leaders agree, the debate is over.

Critics say permanent daylight saving time would mean dark winter mornings. But mornings are already dark in winter for many people, and we all adjust. A little darkness at breakfast is a small price to pay for sunlight when we can actually enjoy it.

Let's stop changing the clocks, keep the light, and give every American an extra hour of evening sunshine.

stimuli.title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time Is a Mistake We Have Already Made
stimuli.source: By Dr. Maya Okonkwo, sleep medicine physician. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Almost everyone agrees that changing the clocks twice a year is a nuisance, and on that point I agree. The research on the spring shift is clear: in the days after we lose an hour of sleep, studies have found increases in car crashes and heart attacks. But the solution that is gaining popularity, permanent daylight saving time, would trade a twice-yearly problem for a daily one.

Our bodies run on an internal clock that is set mainly by morning light. Standard time keeps the clock on the wall roughly matched to the sun, with the sun near its highest point around noon. Daylight saving time shifts that schedule an hour later. In summer, the effect is mild. In winter, it means waking, commuting, and starting school in darkness. Under permanent daylight saving time, the sun would not rise in Detroit until about 9:00 a.m. in early January. Without morning light, many people's internal clocks drift later, leaving them with less sleep night after night. For this reason, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine has called for permanent standard time, not permanent daylight saving time.

We do not have to guess how Americans would feel about dark winter mornings, because we have tried it. In January 1974, during an energy crisis, Congress put the country on year-round daylight saving time. The plan was popular when it passed. But as children waited for school buses in the dark that winter, public support dropped sharply. In October 1974, less than a year after the experiment began, Congress returned the country to standard time for the winter months.

Supporters promise that brighter evenings will boost shopping and reduce crime. These claims are uncertain at best. Much of the shopping evidence comes from business groups that would profit from the change, and the energy savings promised in 1974 turned out to be small and hard to measure. Meanwhile, the costs of dark mornings fall on people who have no choice about when they start their day: students, shift workers, and early commuters.

The popularity of a bill is not proof that it is wise. In 1974, Congress made the same promise of brighter evenings, and the public changed its mind within months. Ending the twice-yearly clock change is a good idea. Ending it on standard time is the way to do it.

stimuli.title: The Machine That Multiplied Words
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep. Quotation from Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), in a public-domain English translation.
stimuli.html:
[1] Before the middle of the 1400s, a book in Europe was a rare and costly object. Every copy had to be written out by hand, usually by trained scribes, many of them monks working in monastery workshops. Copying a single long book could take months. As a result, books were owned mainly by churches, universities, and wealthy families, and most Europeans would never own one.

[2] Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg began printing with a system he had spent years developing. His key invention was not the press itself; screw presses had long been used to squeeze grapes for wine and olives for oil. Instead, Gutenberg's breakthrough was a method for casting large numbers of small metal letters, or type, quickly and in identical sizes. A printer could arrange these letters into a page, ink them, press paper against them, and then take the page apart and reuse the letters for the next one. Gutenberg also developed an oil-based ink that clung to metal better than the water-based inks scribes used.

[3] Gutenberg was not the first person to print with movable type. Around the 1040s, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng made type from baked clay, and by the 1200s, Korean printers were casting type in metal. However, Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, which made movable type far less practical there than it was for European languages written with only a few dozen letters. Whether Gutenberg knew of these Asian inventions is uncertain; most historians believe he developed his method independently.

[4] The best-known product of Gutenberg's shop was a Latin Bible, completed around 1455. Scholars estimate that about 180 copies were printed. That number may seem small today, but a team of scribes would have needed years to produce as many.

[5] The new technology spread with remarkable speed. Printers trained in Mainz carried their skills to other cities, and by 1500, presses were operating in more than 200 towns across Europe. Historians estimate that these presses had produced millions of books by that year. As supply rose, prices fell, and books came within reach of merchants, lawyers, teachers, and skilled workers.

[6] Cheaper books changed more than who could read. Before printing, every hand-copied text was slightly different, and errors multiplied as copies were made from copies. Printing allowed readers in different cities to study exactly the same words, maps, and diagrams. Scientists could compare observations and correct one another's mistakes in later editions. Printing also gave new ideas a speed they had never had. When Martin Luther, a German monk, challenged the practices of the Catholic Church in 1517, printed copies of his arguments spread across Germany within weeks, helping to launch the Protestant Reformation.

[7] Not everyone celebrated. Some scholars complained that printers, eager for profit, rushed out books full of errors. Religious and political authorities, alarmed by the flood of pamphlets they could not control, began requiring printers to obtain licenses and banning works they considered dangerous. These efforts slowed the spread of some ideas, but they could not stop it; a book banned in one city could often be printed in another.

[8] More than a century and a half after Gutenberg, the English writer Francis Bacon named printing as one of three inventions, along with gunpowder and the magnetic compass, that had transformed the world. These three, he wrote, “have changed the whole face and state of things throughout the world.” Few historians today would disagree. In many ways, our current arguments about how quickly information travels online echo debates that began in a print shop in Mainz.

stimuli.title: Maple Street Community Garden: 2027 Plot Agreement
stimuli.source: Original workplace and community document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
1. Plot Sizes and Fees. Raised bed (4 feet by 8 feet): $25 per season. In-ground plot (10 feet by 10 feet): $40 per season. Households that receive SNAP or WIC benefits pay half of the listed fee. Each household may rent no more than one in-ground plot and no more than two raised beds.

2. Season Dates. The garden season runs from April 1 through November 15. Plots must be cleared of all plants, stakes, and debris by November 15.

3. Planting Deadline. Every plot must be planted by May 15. Plots that are not planted by that date will be offered to the next household on the waiting list, and the fee will not be refunded.

4. Work Hours. Each household agrees to contribute 6 hours of volunteer work per season to shared tasks, such as weeding paths, turning compost, and repairing tools. Work hours may be completed at any of the monthly work days or by arrangement with the garden coordinator.

5. Water. Hoses may be used only between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m. and between 5:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. Please turn off spigots completely after use.

6. Garden Rules. No chemical pesticides or weed killers may be used anywhere in the garden. Tall plants such as corn and sunflowers must be planted on the north side of a plot so that they do not shade neighboring plots.

7. Notices. A gardener who is not following this agreement will receive a written notice from the garden coordinator. A gardener who receives two written notices in the same season will lose his or her plot for the rest of the season.

8. Contacts. Questions about plots, fees, and work days should be directed to the garden coordinator, Rosa Delgado. Report broken spigots or fence damage to the Parks Department at 555-0148.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Community gardens first became popular during the world wars, when the government asked Americans to grow their own food.
Community gardens can provide food and strengthen neighborhoods, but many need secure land and steady leadership to survive.
Studies prove that joining a community garden causes people to eat better and exercise more.
Cities should transfer all of their vacant lots to land trusts so that the lots can be turned into gardens.
items.explain:
The passage describes the benefits of gardens (food in paragraph 3, health and social ties in paragraph 4, changes to the block in paragraph 5), then the reasons many gardens fail (borrowed land and too few organizers in paragraph 6), and ways to protect them (paragraph 7). The conclusion ties these together: a garden can be very productive if it has “a secure claim to the land.”

The world wars are background in paragraph 2, not the main point. Paragraph 4 says the study does not prove the garden caused the differences. The passage describes land trusts as one step some cities take; it never says all vacant lots should be transferred.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
options: to argue that the government should again ask Americans to plant victory gardens
to explain why most community gardens are built on land the gardeners do not own
to show that community gardens grew more food in the 1940s than they do today
to show that shared gardening had a long history in the United States before the modern movement began
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 opens, “The idea is not new,” then describes victory gardens in both world wars and says the modern movement began in the 1970s. It gives historical background.

The paragraph makes no argument for a new government campaign, does not discuss land ownership (that is paragraph 6), and never compares the 1940s harvest with today's.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that identifies a limitation of the study's findings.
spans: Researchers have also looked for benefits that are harder to weigh.
In one study, a team surveyed 400 adults in a mid-sized city, about half of whom belonged to a community garden.
The gardeners reported eating more vegetables, exercising more, and knowing more of their neighbors by name than the non-gardeners did.

The researchers noted, however, that people who choose to join a garden may already be more active and more social than people who do not, so the garden itself may not be responsible for all of the differences.
items.explain:
The last sentence warns that gardeners may have been more active and social before they joined, so “the garden itself may not be responsible for all of the differences.” That is a limitation: the study cannot show that gardening caused the results.

The third sentence reports the results but does not question them.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, the author refers to “benefits that are harder to weigh.” In this context, the phrase means benefits that—
options: are difficult to measure, unlike pounds of vegetables
matter less than the food a garden produces
are disputed by the researchers who study them
take many years to appear
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 measures a garden's harvest in “dozens of pounds of vegetables.” Paragraph 4 then turns to benefits such as better diet, more exercise, and knowing neighbors, which cannot be put on a scale. “Harder to weigh” plays on the idea of weighing a harvest: these benefits are harder to measure.

The author does not say these benefits matter less, the researchers do not dispute them (they only caution about the cause), and nothing in the paragraph is about time.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 6, which problems often cause community gardens to fail? Select two answers.
options: Insects and plant diseases destroy the harvest.
Owners sell or build on the land when property values rise.
Seeds and tools become too expensive for gardeners.
Cities stop providing water to garden lots.
The few volunteers who organize the garden move away.
Neighbors complain about noise from work days.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 names two problems: land (“When property values rise, owners may decide to sell or build”) and volunteers (“When the two or three people who organize work days and collect fees move away, a garden can fall apart”).

Pests, the cost of seeds, water service, and noise complaints are never mentioned.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 7, why would a long-term lease encourage gardeners to plant fruit trees?
options: Fruit trees are required by most land trusts.
A lease allows gardeners to sell their fruit for profit.
Gardeners would be more confident that they will still have the land when the trees begin to produce.
Fruit trees need less care than vegetables do.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 says leases and land trusts “give gardeners a reason to invest in soil, sheds, and fruit trees that take years to pay off.” A tree that takes years to bear fruit is only worth planting if the gardeners expect to keep the land that long. Paragraph 6 explains the risk: a garden “can be bulldozed in a day.”

The passage never says land trusts require fruit trees, mentions selling fruit, or compares the care that trees and vegetables need.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, classify each statement as a benefit of community gardens or a challenge they face. Drag each statement into the correct box.
choices: Gardeners share extra produce with food pantries and senior centers.
Gardens are often built on borrowed land.
Older residents teach younger neighbors gardening skills.
A garden may depend on only two or three organizers.
A vacant lot becomes a place where people gather after work.
items.explain:
Benefits: sharing produce (paragraph 3), older residents teaching younger ones, and lots that become gathering places (paragraph 5).

Challenges: paragraph 6 explains that gardens on borrowed land can be lost when owners sell or build, and that a garden run by “two or three people” can fall apart when they move away.

items.prompt: How does paragraph 7 relate to paragraph 6?
options: Paragraph 6 describes problems that threaten gardens, and paragraph 7 describes ways some cities have addressed them.
Paragraph 7 gives evidence that the problems in paragraph 6 have been exaggerated.
Paragraph 7 provides historical background for the problems described in paragraph 6.
Paragraph 6 makes a claim that paragraph 7 proves with research results.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 explains why “many gardens do not survive” (borrowed land and few organizers). Paragraph 7 begins, “Some cities have responded,” and lists zoning protection, land trusts, and long-term leases. This is a problem-and-solution structure.

Paragraph 7 does not deny the problems (it says the steps “do not guarantee success”), gives no history, and contains no research results.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view on community gardens?
options: The author believes gardens are a passing trend that will fade as land values rise.
The author believes gardens could end hunger if cities provided enough land.
The author sees real value in gardens while recognizing their limits and challenges.
The author offers no opinion about whether gardens are worthwhile.
items.explain:
The final paragraph shows both sides of the author's view: a garden “will not end hunger or fix every problem,” but it can become “one of the most productive places on the block.” The author also points out the study's limits (paragraph 4) and the reasons gardens fail (paragraph 6).

The author directly says gardens will not end hunger, does not call them a passing trend, and clearly does offer an opinion in the conclusion.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the narrator says Marcus “believed that if he said something calmly enough, it became true.” What does this suggest about Marcus?
options: He is completely confident that he will pass the swim test.
He is trying to hide his nervousness by acting calm.
He often tells lies to get out of trouble.
He does not understand what the swim test requires.
items.explain:
Marcus says calmly, “I'm getting ready,” right after changing his trunks twice to put off the test. He has failed the test twice (paragraph 4) and later grips the ladder rail with both hands (paragraph 6). His calm words cover up how nervous he is.

His stalling shows he is not truly confident. Nothing suggests he lies to avoid trouble, and the story makes clear he knows exactly what the test requires.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the narrator describes the water as “a sheet of hammered tin.” This description helps the reader picture the water as—
options: rough and full of waves
dark and cold
crowded with swimmers
flat and shining in the sunlight
items.explain:
The same sentence says the water “lay flat and bright under the August sun.” A sheet of tin is flat and reflects light, so the metaphor shows a still, glaring surface.

A flat sheet is the opposite of rough waves, “bright” rules out dark, and the description says nothing about other swimmers.

items.prompt: In paragraph 9, the narrator tells Marcus, “Water is water.” In paragraph 10, the narrator remembers, “My father had not told me water was water.” What does this contrast reveal?
options: The narrator realizes that giving orders is not how the narrator was helped through the same fear.
The narrator believes the father made swimming seem harder than it really was.
The narrator thinks Marcus is more afraid than the narrator ever was.
The narrator wants Marcus to learn to swim the way their mother taught them.
items.explain:
The narrator has been giving Marcus orders (“Let go,” “Water is water”). Then the narrator remembers that the father did something different: he climbed in and floated calmly, showing rather than telling. The contrast leads the narrator to change approach in paragraph 13 and do what the father did.

The narrator admires the father's way, does not criticize it. Paragraph 10 shows the narrator once had the very same fear (“It was mine”), and the mother never taught anyone to swim in the story.

items.prompt: Paragraph 10 is shown below. Click the sentence that reveals what the narrator, as a child, believed about the deep end.
spans: He looked at me then, and I recognized the look, though it took me a second to remember where I had seen it.
Eight years earlier, I had stood on that same ladder, gripping that same rail, while my father crouched on the deck above me.
I had been sure that the deep end was a different kind of water, heavier and darker, that it wanted to pull me down.
My father had not told me water was water.
He had climbed into the pool in his work clothes, boots and all, and floated beside me on his back with his arms spread wide, looking up at the sky as if he had all afternoon.
items.explain:
The fourth sentence states the child's belief directly: the narrator “had been sure that the deep end was a different kind of water, heavier and darker, that it wanted to pull me down.”

The sentence about gripping the rail shows the narrator's position on the ladder, but it does not say what the narrator believed about the water.

items.prompt: In paragraph 12, the narrator says the memory had been folded away “the way you fold away a coat in summer and forget you own it.” This comparison suggests that the memory—
options: was so painful that the narrator tried to get rid of it
had never really happened and was only imagined
had been set aside rather than lost, and was still there when the narrator needed it
belonged to Marcus rather than to the narrator
items.explain:
A coat put away in summer is not thrown out; it is simply not needed for a while, and it is still there when cold weather returns. In the same way, the memory of the father in the pool was stored away until the narrator needed it to help Marcus.

Nothing suggests the memory was painful or imagined; the father confirms it in paragraph 19 (“Boots and all”). The memory is the narrator's own.

items.prompt: In paragraph 17, the narrator stays on their back and says “nothing at all, which was the hardest thing I did that summer.” This statement suggests that the narrator—
options: was too cold and tired to speak
was annoyed that Marcus was splashing
did not want the lifeguard to hear
had to hold back the urge to coach Marcus so that he could succeed on his own
items.explain:
Earlier, the narrator kept telling Marcus what to do (paragraphs 7 and 9). Staying silent is “the hardest thing” because the narrator wants to help but now understands that Marcus needs to do it himself, with only a calm example nearby. Paragraph 18 supports this: when Marcus does not look back, the narrator decides “that was all right.”

The story gives no sign that the narrator is too tired to talk, annoyed, or hiding from the lifeguard.

items.prompt: Which actions show the narrator following the father's example from years earlier? Select two answers.
options: promising their mother to get Marcus through the test before school
reminding Marcus that they had practiced all week
getting into the pool in shorts and a T-shirt instead of a swimsuit
floating on their back with arms spread wide near the ladder
calling their father on the phone that night
telling Marcus that water is water
items.explain:
In paragraph 10, the father “climbed into the pool in his work clothes” and “floated beside me on his back with his arms spread wide.” In paragraph 13, the narrator slides in while “still wearing my shorts and T-shirt,” then leans back, spreads both arms, and floats. These two actions copy the father.

The promise to the mother, the reminder about practice, and “water is water” are what the narrator did before remembering the father. The phone call happens later and is not something the father did at the pool.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Children should be pushed hard so that they learn to overcome their fears.
Sometimes the best way to help someone through a fear is to show calm by example rather than to give orders.
Family members who move away soon forget the people they left behind.
Passing a test matters less than having fun with friends.
items.explain:
Marcus does not let go of the rail when the narrator gives orders. He lets go only after the narrator quietly floats nearby, just as the father once did. The narrator's silence (paragraph 17) and Marcus's success show that a calm example helped more than instructions.

Pushing Marcus did not work. The father lives far away but still remembers (“Boots and all”). The story never weighs tests against fun.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The cost of medical premiums for employees and their families {{0}} by about 4 percent.”

options: rise
are rising
is rising
have risen

items.explain:
The subject is cost, which is singular. The phrase “of medical premiums for employees and their families” comes between the subject and the verb but does not change the subject. A singular subject needs a singular verb: The cost … is rising.

“Rise,” “are rising,” and “have risen” are plural forms that wrongly agree with “premiums” or “families.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Each plan has {{0}} own deductible, so please compare your options carefully before making a choice.”

options: it's
its
its'
their

items.explain:
The deductible belongs to the plan, so the sentence needs the possessive pronoun its, which has no apostrophe.

“It's” means “it is.” “Its'” is not a word. “Their” is plural and does not agree with the singular “Each plan.”

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the notice. Choose the transition that best connects them.

“Many employees have asked for more mental health options. {{0}}, the new Silver plan includes twelve counseling visits per year at no cost.”

options: In response
Nevertheless
Similarly
On the other hand

items.explain:
Employees asked for more mental health options, and the new plan provides them. The second sentence is an answer to the request, so In response is correct.

“Nevertheless” and “On the other hand” signal a contrast, but the two sentences agree. “Similarly” signals a likeness between two separate things, but the counseling visits are a reply to the request, not something like it.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Employees who do not make changes will keep their current plans, {{0}} for the flexible spending account, which must be renewed every year.”

options: accept
except
expect
excepted

items.explain:
Except means “other than” or “leaving out.” Employees keep every current plan other than the flexible spending account, which must be renewed.

“Accept” means “to receive or agree to,” “expect” means “to think something will happen,” and “excepted” is a verb form that does not fit after the comma.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“A benefits fair will be held in the cafeteria on {{0}} from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.”

options: wednesday, November 4
Wednesday, november 4
Wednesday, November 4
Wednesday November, 4

items.explain:
Days of the week and months are proper nouns, so both are capitalized. A comma separates the day of the week from the date: Wednesday, November 4.

The first two choices leave one name lowercase. The last choice puts the comma between the month and the day number.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Attendance at the fair is optional{{0}} we strongly encourage anyone who is considering a new plan to attend.”

options: , however,
; however,
however
, however

items.explain:
“Attendance at the fair is optional” and “we strongly encourage anyone … to attend” are both independent clauses. When a word like however connects two independent clauses, it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it: optional; however, we.

Commas alone create a comma splice, and leaving out punctuation creates a run-on sentence.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“To make sure that your coverage begins on January 1{{0}} submit your choices through the benefits portal by 5:00 p.m. on November 20.”

options: . Please
, please
; please
and please

items.explain:
“To make sure that your coverage begins on January 1” is an introductory phrase, not a complete sentence. It should be joined to the main clause with a comma: January 1, please submit.

A period leaves the introductory phrase as a fragment. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the phrase cannot stand alone. “And please” joins a phrase to a command as if they were equal parts, which makes the sentence ungrammatical.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you have questions, please contact Darnell Price or {{0}} in Human Resources.”

options: I
me
myself
mine

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the verb “contact,” so it must be an object pronoun: me. Test it by removing “Darnell Price or”: “please contact me,” not “please contact I.”

“Myself” is used only when the subject of the sentence is the same person (“I did it myself”), and “mine” is possessive.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of making daylight saving time permanent in the United States.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I learned about the opening from Ms. Joy Tran, {{0}} I worked with for two years at Valley Home Supply.”

options: who
whom
which
whose

items.explain:
The pronoun is the object of the preposition “with” (I worked with her). Object pronouns that refer to people use whom. Test it by rewording: “I worked with her,” so “whom.”

“Who” is a subject pronoun (“she worked”). “Which” refers to things, not people, and “whose” shows possession.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“In that role, I trained new hires, managed weekly inventory counts, and {{0}}.”

options: resolving customer complaints
I was resolving customer complaints
resolved customer complaints
customer complaints were resolved by me

items.explain:
Items in a series should have the same grammatical form. The first two items are past-tense verbs (“trained,” “managed”), so the third must be one too: resolved customer complaints.

“Resolving” is an -ing form, and the other two choices are full clauses, one in the passive voice, so they break the pattern.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“My two {{0}} evaluations both praised my ability to stay organized during our busiest seasons.”

options: supervisor's
supervisors'
supervisors
supervisors's

items.explain:
“Two” tells us there is more than one supervisor, and the evaluations belong to them. A plural noun ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe after the s: supervisors'.

“Supervisor's” is singular possessive (one supervisor), “supervisors” is plural with no possession, and “supervisors's” is not a correct form.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, customer satisfaction scores at our store rose by 12 percent in six months.”

options: After introducing a new returns process
After I introduced a new returns process
Having introduced a new returns process
Introducing a new returns process

items.explain:
An introductory phrase without its own subject describes the noun that comes right after the comma, which here is “customer satisfaction scores.” Scores cannot introduce a process, so the phrase must name who did it: After I introduced a new returns process, customer satisfaction scores rose.

The other three choices are dangling modifiers. Each one says, in effect, that the scores introduced the new returns process.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I would bring three strengths to {{0}}, experience leading a team, and a commitment to helpful service.”

options: Greenleaf: product knowledge
Greenleaf; product knowledge
Greenleaf, product knowledge
Greenleaf product knowledge

items.explain:
“I would bring three strengths to Greenleaf” is a complete sentence that announces a list. A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence: Greenleaf: product knowledge, experience leading a team, and a commitment to helpful service.

A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the list is not a clause. A comma makes it look as if “Greenleaf” is the first item in the list. With no punctuation, “Greenleaf product knowledge” runs the company name into the first strength, so the list is no longer set off from the sentence that introduces it.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I have worked in home improvement retail for more {{0}} six years, and I enjoy helping customers find the right tool for each job.”

options: then
than
that
as

items.explain:
Than is used to make comparisons: “more than six years.”

“Then” refers to time (“first this, then that”). “More that” and “more as” are not standard comparisons.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, I recently completed a certificate in retail management at Westlake Community College.”

options: In addition
Instead
For example
Otherwise

items.explain:
The previous paragraph describes the writer's work experience. This sentence adds another qualification, a certificate. In addition signals that new, related information is being added.

“Instead” suggests the certificate replaced the experience, and “Otherwise” suggests a different possible outcome. Earning a certificate is not an example of helping customers find tools, so “For example” does not fit.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Gutenberg deserves sole credit for the invention of movable type.
The printing press was popular with scholars but feared by most ordinary Europeans.
Censorship by religious and political authorities kept printing from spreading new ideas.
Gutenberg's printing method spread quickly and changed who could own books and how fast ideas traveled, despite some resistance.
items.explain:
The passage describes Gutenberg's method (paragraph 2), its rapid spread and falling book prices (paragraph 5), its effects on accuracy and the speed of ideas (paragraph 6), the resistance it met (paragraph 7), and its lasting importance (paragraph 8).

Paragraph 3 says Gutenberg “was not the first person to print with movable type.” Some scholars complained, but the passage does not say ordinary Europeans feared printing. Paragraph 7 says censorship “could not stop” the spread of ideas.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, why does the author mention that screw presses “had long been used to squeeze grapes for wine and olives for oil”?
options: to show that Gutenberg's real breakthrough was his method of making type, not the press itself
to suggest that Gutenberg first worked as a winemaker
to argue that printing was less important than farming
to explain why early printed books were expensive
items.explain:
The sentence begins, “His key invention was not the press itself,” and the detail about wine and oil proves that presses already existed. The next sentence then names the real breakthrough: “a method for casting large numbers of small metal letters.”

Gutenberg is called a goldsmith, not a winemaker. The detail does not compare printing with farming or explain book prices.

items.prompt: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word independently most nearly means—
options: quickly and carelessly
with money from wealthy supporters
without relying on the work of others
in secret from the authorities
items.explain:
The sentence says it is uncertain whether Gutenberg “knew of these Asian inventions” and that most historians believe he developed his method independently, that is, on his own, without building on the earlier Chinese and Korean work.

The context is about whether he knew of others' inventions, not about speed, money, or secrecy.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, why was movable type less practical in China than in Europe?
options: Chinese printers did not know how to cast type in metal.
Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, while European languages use only a few dozen letters.
Clay type broke too easily to be used more than once.
Chinese rulers banned printing with movable type.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 states that Chinese writing “uses thousands of different characters, which made movable type far less practical there than it was for European languages written with only a few dozen letters.” A printer would need far more different pieces of type.

The passage says Korean printers cast metal type and never says clay type broke or that rulers banned movable type.

items.prompt: Put these events from the passage in the order in which they happened. Drag each event into the correct position.
choices: Printed copies of Martin Luther's arguments spread across Germany.
Bi Sheng makes movable type from baked clay.
Francis Bacon names printing as a world-changing invention.
Gutenberg's shop completes a Latin Bible.
Korean printers cast type in metal.
items.explain: (1) Bi Sheng's clay type, around the 1040s; (2) Korean metal type, by the 1200s; (3) the Gutenberg Bible, around 1455; (4) Luther's printed arguments, 1517; (5) Bacon, “more than a century and a half after Gutenberg” (his book appeared in 1620).

items.prompt: According to paragraph 6, which changes resulted from printing? Select two answers.
options: Readers in different cities could study exactly the same words, maps, and diagrams.
Hand-copied books became more accurate than before.
Scientists could correct one another's mistakes in later editions.
Authorities stopped requiring printers to have licenses.
Monks stopped copying books by hand.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 says printing “allowed readers in different cities to study exactly the same words, maps, and diagrams” and that scientists “could compare observations and correct one another's mistakes in later editions.”

The paragraph says hand-copied texts were full of differences and errors, not that they improved. Paragraph 7 says authorities began requiring licenses. The passage never says monks stopped copying.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 is shown below. Click the sentence that explains why attempts to control printing were not fully successful.
spans: Some scholars complained that printers, eager for profit, rushed out books full of errors.
Religious and political authorities, alarmed by the flood of pamphlets they could not control, began requiring printers to obtain licenses and banning works they considered dangerous.
These efforts slowed the spread of some ideas, but they could not stop it; a book banned in one city could often be printed in another.
items.explain:
The last sentence says the efforts “could not stop” the spread of ideas and gives the reason: “a book banned in one city could often be printed in another.”

The third sentence describes the attempts at control (licenses and bans) but does not say why they fell short.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 4.

“That number may seem small today, but a team of scribes would have needed years to produce as many.”

Why does the author include this sentence?
options: to criticize Gutenberg for printing so few copies
to suggest that scribes were more skilled than printers
to explain why the Gutenberg Bible was written in Latin
to help readers understand how much faster printing was than copying by hand
items.explain:
About 180 copies sounds small to a modern reader. The author compares that number with the years scribes would have needed to make as many, which shows how great a speed-up printing was.

The sentence does not criticize Gutenberg, rank scribes' skill, or explain the choice of Latin.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 8?
options: to show that printing's importance was recognized long ago and still connects to debates today
to argue that the internet is more important than the printing press
to prove that gunpowder and the compass mattered more than printing
to suggest that Francis Bacon helped develop the printing press
items.explain:
Paragraph 8 quotes Bacon, writing more than 150 years after Gutenberg, on how printing “changed the whole face and state of things throughout the world,” says “Few historians today would disagree,” and links today's arguments about online information to “debates that began in a print shop in Mainz.” It shows printing's lasting importance.

The paragraph does not rank the internet above printing or rank Bacon's three inventions, and Bacon wrote long after printing was developed.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 says that “a book banned in one city could often be printed in another.” What can the reader infer from this statement?
options: Printers in other cities could not read the banned books.
Banned books were usually printed only in Mainz.
An authority's power to ban books usually reached only as far as the area it controlled.
Most authorities wanted banned ideas to spread.
items.explain:
If a ban in one city did not stop printing in another, the banning authority must not have controlled the other city. Each authority's ban applied only within its own area, so printers elsewhere could keep publishing.

Nothing suggests printers could not read, and paragraph 5 says presses operated in more than 200 towns, not only Mainz. The authorities described in paragraph 7 were “alarmed” by ideas they could not control, so they did not want them to spread.

items.prompt: The Jackson household receives SNAP benefits and wants to rent one in-ground plot and one raised bed. According to the agreement, how much will the household pay for the season?
items.explain:
Section 1 lists the fees and allows one in-ground plot plus up to two raised beds.

Full price: $40 + $25 = $65.

Households that receive SNAP pay half: $65 ÷ 2 = $32.50.

$65.00 forgets the discount, $20.00 counts only the in-ground plot at half price, and $52.50 ($40 + $12.50) applies the discount to only the raised bed.

items.prompt: According to the agreement, which gardener is breaking a rule?
options: a gardener who waters with a hose at 7:00 p.m.
a gardener who plants sunflowers on the north side of a plot
a gardener who completes work hours by arrangement with the coordinator
a gardener who waters with a hose at 1:00 p.m.
items.explain:
Section 5 allows hoses “only between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m. and between 5:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m.” 1:00 p.m. falls outside both windows.

7:00 p.m. is inside the evening window. Section 6 requires tall plants such as sunflowers to go on the north side. Section 4 allows work hours to be done “by arrangement with the garden coordinator.”

items.prompt: A gardener paid her fee in April but has not planted anything in her plot by May 16. According to section 3, what will happen?
options: Her plot will be offered to the next household on the waiting list, and her fee will not be refunded.
She will receive one written notice and may keep her plot until she receives a second notice.
Her fee will be refunded, and she may apply again next season.
She must complete 6 additional work hours to keep her plot.
items.explain:
Section 3 says every plot must be planted by May 15, and plots not planted by that date “will be offered to the next household on the waiting list, and the fee will not be refunded.” May 16 is past the deadline.

The two-notice rule in section 7 covers general violations; section 3 sets the specific result for missing the planting deadline. The fee is not refunded, and the agreement never trades extra work hours for a plot.

items.prompt: According to section 8, whom should a gardener contact in each situation? Drag each situation into the correct box.
choices: a question about the date of the next work day
a spigot that is broken and will not turn off
a question about whether a household qualifies for the half-price fee
a section of fence knocked down by a fallen branch
a question about which plot has been assigned
items.explain: Section 8 sends “questions about plots, fees, and work days” to the garden coordinator: the work-day question, the fee question, and the plot question. It sends “broken spigots or fence damage” to the Parks Department: the broken spigot and the fallen fence.
